newsitem.title: USA: Motorola's rosy outlook triggers gains in stock.
newsitem.headline: Motorola's rosy outlook triggers gains in stock.

text.p: The stock of technology giant Motorola Inc. rose in active trading after the company gave the market a more promising outlook for its mobile phone and semiconductor businesses.

"It seems like in a number of Motorola businesses, business trends have troughed and are starting to improve," Lehman Bros. analyst Todd Koffman said, adding that wireless phones and semiconductors in particular showed promise.
"Those are Motorola's main two earnings-driver segments," Koffman said.

Late Thursday, Schaumburg, Ill.-based Motorola reported a fall of about 45 percent in profits in the fourth quarter compared with last year, but the company also indicated the key businesses were picking up after struggling through 1996.
Ed Gams, director of investor relations for Motorola, told analysts in a conference call the company does not expect a return to overall increased profitability until later this year.
But talk of a rebound sparked analysts' upgrades and a surge in the stock.

"It has been down in the doldrums for so long that (on) any sign of good news, people ... just take it all the way up," said Rakesh Sood, an analyst for Hambrecht & Quist, a brokerage and investment bank.
Sood raised his rating to buy from hold -- one of many analysts who upgraded the stock.

In addition to a positive outlook, analysts said the overall results beat expectations. Motorola reported fourth-quarter net earnings of $238 million, including more than $150 million in pretax charges, vs. $432 million last year.
Motorola rose $1.50 to $66.50 in composite trading. It was the most actively traded stock on the New York Stock Exchange.

Sales in Motorola's General Systems Segment, which includes wireless phones, rose 17 percent in the fourth quarter and orders were up 21 percent vs. last year -- gains which analysts said were larger than anticipated.
Analysts said they were encouraged by the market's acceptance of Motorola's new digital mobile phones.

The U.S. market, for example, is in the process of switching to digital from analogue, and the company said it expected some of its new digital phones to give it a very strong market position in the United States.
In fact, Motorola's Gams said overall demand for some of the new phones during the fourth quarter exceeded the company's ability to produce them.
"We're going to ramp volumes up, but a quick snap back in market share probably isn't going to happen," Gams said, citing competition in the market.

In the wireless phone market, Motorola's market share remains high but has decreased. According to analysts, Motorola's current share worldwide in mobile phones is about 38 percent -- down from an estimated 45 percent in 1995.

The semiconductor sector posted the results analysts said they were hoping for. Although sales and orders were lower compared to last year, the company posted larger-than-expected gains from the third quarter. Motorola said fourth-quarter orders were up more than 20 percent compared with the third.

"You really have to look for sequential improvements," said Mona Eraiba, an analyst for Gruntal & Co., a brokerage and investment bank. "I think the underlying numbers are very clear that things are improving."
Even Motorola, which analysts said is known for its conservative projections, surrendered to cautious optimism.
"We continue to believe the recovery from the semiconductor industry recessionary cycle of 1996 has begun; however, we also continue to believe that the recovery will be gradual," Gams said.
